detail:
The CDC states plainly that there is no cure or approved treatment for ME/CFS, so management aims at the symptoms that cause the most problems, decided together by the person, their family, and their healthcare providers. For post-exertional malaise, the CDC describes activity management, also called pacing, as one of the best options: find individual limits for mental and physical activity, then plan activity and rest to stay within them, an approach patients call staying within the energy envelope.

The CDC suggests practical steps such as keeping a daily diary of symptoms and activities for 1 to 2 weeks to spot patterns, breaking tasks into pieces, and scheduling rest after exertion. It also cautions that people with ME/CFS do not tolerate vigorous aerobic exercise routines, which is why pacing, not pushing through, is the recommended frame.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor before changing your activity plan.
summary: CDC guidance centers ME/CFS care on pacing: learning personal activity limits and planning physical, mental, and emotional exertion to stay inside them, because there is no cure or approved treatment for the disease itself.
takeaways: pacing means planning activity and rest around your limits
pem can start 12 to 48 hours after exertion and last days
a 1 to 2 week activity and symptom diary can reveal limits
care targets the most disruptive symptoms first; review plans with your doctor
title: Pacing: the core ME/CFS management strategy
